4: Thirteen [is the age] for [observing] commandments: As it is written, When a man or woman shall commit any sin that people commit, etc. (Numbers 5:6). But he is not called a man until he is thirteen, as we find there: Simeon and Levi, Dinah's brothers, took [each man his sword] (Genesis 34:25). And Levi was thirteen years old then, if you calculate the two years Jacob spent in Bet El. A different version: Thirteen [is the age] for [observing] commandments, as one who grows two [pubic] hairs has reached the category of [those who are required to observe] the commandments from Torah writ. As this is a law of Moses from [Mount] Sinai. And the sages estimated the growth of two hairs at thirteen years of age. Hence we bring him into the performance of commandments [at that age]. And from that time onwards, we hold that it is likely that he has two hairs, like most youths. However, if we know clearly that he has not yet grown two hairs at thirteen, he is not obligated [to observe the] commandments from Torah writ, but only rabbinically for education, since we educate a child already from six, already from ten. As regarding Torah writ, we wait for him until he is twenty, perhaps he will grow two hairs. But if he reaches twenty and did not grow [them], he revealed about himself that he is a eunuch. As a eunuch does not have two hairs, yet he is obligated in all of the commandments and all of the punishments in the Torah. And that is [the meaning of] what we learned further, "Twenty [is the age] for pursuing": That once he has reached the category of [those who are] twenty, the court would pursue him to punish him with rabbinic lashes for rebellion [if it is warranted] in order to discipline him regarding all the designated death penalties and punishments. It makes no difference if he has grown [the hairs] or has not grown [them], and from twenty onwards, Scripture considers him to be like any man. As it is written, From the age of twenty years up (Numbers 1:3).
